top_learned_concepts: Core OS infrastructure cluster: operating systems, virtualization, hypervisors, Hyper-V, and how resources relate across hardware/OS/application layers.
Containerization and environment packaging: Docker and the idea that containers bundle what an application needs to run.
Testing and quality workflows: unit tests, CI, and how tests support server-side development.
Platform/tool awareness: some students specifically noticed Windows-based virtualization tools and system-level tooling.
top_struggle_clusters: Concept boundary confusion between related technologies: students seem unsure how VMs, hypervisors, containers, and virtualization differ and relate.
Testing design transfer: students are asking less about syntax and more about what tests to write, how testing differs across languages, and how to test apps, APIs, databases, and bots.
CI/CD at team scale: uncertainty about GitHub pushing workflows, merge conflicts, branch protection, and what CI actually catches when multiple developers contribute.
System/networking details remain fuzzy: Hyper-V networking, virtual switches, checkpoints, and the consequences of not having a hypervisor.
Big-picture integration challenge: some reflections suggest the topics feel broad and disconnected, making it hard to see how all the pieces fit in real development environments.
future_interest_clusters: Broader OS exposure, especially Linux or comparing non-Windows environments.
Deeper virtualization topics, including checkpoints and VM infrastructure behavior.
Applied testing beyond basic unit tests: APIs, databases, SQL, bots, and realistic server-side projects.
CI/CD continuation into deployment: interest in the CD side, including automated deployment to cloud platforms.
Collaboration workflows for larger projects using GitHub.
mismatches: Unit testing appears in both learned and struggled themes, suggesting students grasp the basic idea but lack confidence applying it to authentic project components.
Docker/containerization was perceived as learned by some students, but others still question its importance and want more depth, indicating uneven buy-in or understanding of use cases.
Virtualization/hypervisor content registered as a key takeaway, yet students still seem unclear on distinctions among VMs, hypervisors, and related infrastructure details.
Students reported learning CI, but struggle responses show unresolved confusion about how CI behaves in multi-developer, real-company workflows.
Difficulty ratings are moderately high overall (mean 5.82, median 6) despite many concrete learning takeaways, which fits a pattern of successful exposure but incomplete conceptual integration.
teaching_adjustments: Teach a comparison matrix or diagram for hypervisors vs VMs vs containers vs host OS, with one concrete example stack students can revisit.
Add a short 'what problem does this solve?' segment for Docker, CI, hypervisors, and virtual networking to address perceived relevance, not just mechanics.
Use one worked project to connect the pipeline end-to-end: write tests, push to GitHub, run CI, resolve a conflicting change scenario, and optionally discuss deployment.
Differentiate testing instruction into levels: what to test, examples of good unit tests, and how strategies change for APIs, databases, bots, and multi-language stacks.
Include a practical collaboration mini-lesson on branching, pull requests, branch protection, merge conflicts, and why passing local tests may still fail after integration.

Provide an architecture-level recap at the end of class that links OS/virtualization/container/testing concepts into one ecosystem view, since several students seem to need the big picture before details fully stick.
followup_exit_ticket_questions: Which distinction is still least clear: hypervisor vs VM, VM vs container, or CI vs CD?
For your current or recent project, what is one component you would want to test but are unsure how to test?
How confident are you that you could explain why a developer would use Docker in a real project? Why?
What part of team-based GitHub workflow feels most unclear right now: branching, pull requests, conflicts, reviews, or CI checks?
Would a Linux-based demo or lab help you understand these topics better than a Windows-only example?
ai_summary.short_instructor_summary: Students perceived substantial learning this week around operating systems, virtualization/hypervisors, Docker, and unit testing/CI. The main struggles were not simple recall problems but application and differentiation problems: how similar technologies relate, what tests to write in realistic systems, and how CI/GitHub workflows behave in collaborative settings. Future interest strongly points toward more Docker, Linux/OS comparison, deeper testing practice, and extending CI into CD/deployment. Instructionally, the clearest opportunity is to unify these topics with a single end-to-end project and explicit comparison frameworks so students can connect the mechanics to the larger software engineering picture.

study_guide.title: Study Guide for 2026-04-19: OS, Virtualization, Docker, Testing, and CI
study_guide.overview: This week introduced several connected infrastructure and software engineering ideas: operating systems, virtualization and hypervisors, Docker/containers, unit testing, and CI workflows. Many students could identify the main ideas, but several reflections showed that the harder part is telling similar tools apart, understanding why they matter, and applying them in realistic projects. Before class, focus on building a clear big-picture map and reviewing how these topics connect in a development workflow.
key_takeaways_to_review: Operating systems manage system resources for applications.
Virtualization and hypervisors relate hardware, operating systems, and resource allocation.
Hyper-V and other virtualization tools are examples students encountered this week.
Containers package what an application needs to run.
Docker is a key example of container-based workflow mentioned by many students.
Unit tests help check whether parts of a program are working correctly.
CI connects code changes and automated testing in a development workflow.
These topics are related: system setup, packaging, testing, and code integration all support building and maintaining software.
common_sticking_points: Keeping the boundaries clear between hypervisors, virtualization, VMs, and containers.
Understanding why Docker is useful beyond just knowing how to run it.
Deciding what unit tests to write for real applications, not just small examples.
Knowing how testing ideas transfer across languages or project types.
Figuring out how to test more complex components like APIs, databases, or bots.
Understanding GitHub/CI workflows when multiple developers push changes.
Seeing the 'big picture' of how OS concepts, containers, testing, and CI fit together.
practice_prompts: Make a simple comparison chart: operating system vs hypervisor vs VM vs container. For each, write what role it plays.
In one or two sentences, explain why a developer might use Docker in a real project.
Think of a recent program you wrote. List 2-3 parts that could be unit tested.
For one feature in a server-side project, describe what you would want to verify with tests.
Write a short workflow summary: code change -> push to GitHub -> tests run in CI -> next step.
Identify one place where team workflows could fail even if individual code changes seem correct.
If the topics feel disconnected, try grouping them by purpose: system resources, environment setup, testing, and collaboration.
self_check_questions: Can I explain the difference between a VM and a container at a high level?
Can I explain what a hypervisor does in relation to hardware and operating systems?
Can I describe one practical reason containers are useful?
Can I give an example of what a unit test checks?
Do I understand that knowing test syntax is different from knowing what should be tested?
Can I describe what CI does after code is pushed?
Do I know which part is least clear to me right now: virtualization concepts, Docker, testing strategy, or team workflow?
before_next_class: Review your notes and identify one distinction that still feels blurry, especially among hypervisors, VMs, containers, CI, and CD.
Bring one example from a current or past project of something you are unsure how to test.
If possible, revisit any Docker or virtualization demo/material and focus on what problem the tool solves.
Think about how a team project on GitHub might need more than just passing tests, such as coordination and review.
Prepare one question about the big-picture connection between systems topics and software development workflow.
